title: Upstart lends to more people with low credit scores, at lower rates
summary: Upstart's machine-learning lending model approved 15 to 30 percent of low-score applicants that traditional models reject, at lower rates; a 2024 monitor found disparities for Black applicants.
account: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau granted its first no-action letter to Upstart Network in September 2017. On 6 August 2019 Patrice Alexander Ficklin and Paul Watkins reported in a bureau blog post on results from the compliance plan attached to that letter. Upstart compared its tested model with a hypothetical traditional model using conventional variables. It reported that the tested model approves 27% more applicants and yields 16% lower average annual percentage rates for approved loans. Acceptance rates were up 23–29% and annual percentage rates down 15–17% across racial, ethnic and sex categories. Near-prime applicants (FICO 620–660) were approved approximately twice as frequently. Applicants under 25 were 32% more likely to be approved and those with incomes under $50,000 13% more likely. The post states that the results for minority, female and 62-and-older applicants show no disparities requiring further fair-lending analysis. The post says that the results reflect the net effect of both the alternative data and the machine-learning methodology. Upstart supplied the analysis. The bureau stated that it did not separately replicate it. In February 2020 the Student Borrower Protection Center reported that Upstart quoted a hypothetical Howard University graduate nearly $3,499 more over a five-year refinancing loan than a similar New York University graduate. On 8 June 2022 the bureau terminated the 2020 no-action letter at Upstart's request after Upstart planned to expand the variables in its model. On 27 March 2024 the NAACP Legal Defense Fund and the Student Borrower Protection Center announced the final report of Relman Colfax, the independent monitor. The report identified approval disparities for Black applicants. It also found some disparities in annual percentage rates for Black, Hispanic and female applicants, but none exceeded its thresholds for practical significance. Upstart rejected the monitor's proposed less discriminatory alternative model. On 13 May 2026 Marco Di Maggio and Dimuthu Ratnadiwakara reported in Management Science that Upstart approves 15 to 30 percent of low-score applicants rejected by traditional models, at lower rates. They found that alternative data drove most of the gains for borrowers with thin credit files and low scores, and that wider access improved borrowers' later finances.

ai_role.statement: The CFPB states that the 2019 gains reflect alternative data and machine learning together. The 2026 Management Science study separates the two. Its authors report that alternative data drove most gains for borrowers with thin credit files and low scores, and that the more complex model added gains where credit reports held more information. Upstart built and ran the model and supplied the data for both analyses.

data.retained_case_account: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau reported results from the compliance plan attached to its first no-action letter, granted to Upstart Network in September 2017. The results were in a 6 August 2019 blog post by Patrice Alexander Ficklin and Paul Watkins. Upstart compared its tested model with a hypothetical traditional model using conventional variables. It reported that the tested model approves 27% more applicants and yields 16% lower average APRs for approved loans. Acceptance rates were up 23–29% and APRs down 15–17% across racial, ethnic and sex categories. Near-prime applicants (FICO 620–660) were approved approximately twice as frequently. Applicants under 25 were 32% more likely to be approved and those with incomes under $50,000 13% more likely. The post states that the results for minority, female and 62-and-older applicants show no disparities requiring further fair-lending analysis. The post says that they reflect the net effect of both the alternative data and the machine-learning methodology. Upstart supplied the analysis. The CFPB expressly stated that it did not separately replicate it. On 8 June 2022 the CFPB terminated the 2020 no-action letter at Upstart's request after Upstart planned to expand the variables in its model. On 27 March 2024 the NAACP Legal Defense Fund and the Student Borrower Protection Center announced Relman Colfax's final independent-monitorship report. The final independent monitor report identified approval disparities for Black applicants. It also found some APR disparities for Black, Hispanic, and female applicants, but none exceeded its practical-significance thresholds. Upstart rejected the monitor's proposed less discriminatory alternative model.

display.answer: Upstart supplied the 2019 approval and rate estimates, and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau published them without replicating them. Upstart also supplied the data for the 2026 Management Science study, and an earlier working-paper version had Upstart's Chief Data Scientist as co-author. The independent monitor and the Student Borrower Protection Center tested the model separately and found disparities.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: Upstart's machine-learning lending model approved 15 to 30 percent of low-score applicants that traditional models reject, at lower rates; a 2024 monitor found disparities for Black applicants.
fields.account: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau granted its first no-action letter to Upstart Network in September 2017. On 6 August 2019 Patrice Alexander Ficklin and Paul Watkins reported in a bureau blog post on results from the compliance plan attached to that letter. Upstart compared its tested model with a hypothetical traditional model using conventional variables. It reported that the tested model approves 27% more applicants and yields 16% lower average annual percentage rates for approved loans. Acceptance rates were up 23–29% and annual percentage rates down 15–17% across racial, ethnic and sex categories. Near-prime applicants (FICO 620–660) were approved approximately twice as frequently. Applicants under 25 were 32% more likely to be approved and those with incomes under $50,000 13% more likely. The post states that the results for minority, female and 62-and-older applicants show no disparities requiring further fair-lending analysis. The post says that the results reflect the net effect of both the alternative data and the machine-learning methodology. Upstart supplied the analysis. The bureau stated that it did not separately replicate it. In February 2020 the Student Borrower Protection Center reported that Upstart quoted a hypothetical Howard University graduate nearly $3,499 more over a five-year refinancing loan than a similar New York University graduate. On 8 June 2022 the bureau terminated the 2020 no-action letter at Upstart's request after Upstart planned to expand the variables in its model. On 27 March 2024 the NAACP Legal Defense Fund and the Student Borrower Protection Center announced the final report of Relman Colfax, the independent monitor. The report identified approval disparities for Black applicants. It also found some disparities in annual percentage rates for Black, Hispanic and female applicants, but none exceeded its thresholds for practical significance. Upstart rejected the monitor's proposed less discriminatory alternative model. On 13 May 2026 Marco Di Maggio and Dimuthu Ratnadiwakara reported in Management Science that Upstart approves 15 to 30 percent of low-score applicants rejected by traditional models, at lower rates. They found that alternative data drove most of the gains for borrowers with thin credit files and low scores, and that wider access improved borrowers' later finances.
